claims.text: What the image looks like Tree-in-bud opacities, centrilobular nodules → endobronchial spread (TB, MAC, aspiration)
claims.quote: Tree-in-bud opacities, centrilobular nodules Endobronchial spread (TB, MAC, aspiration)

claims.text: Buzzword: tree-in-bud on chest CT = endobronchial spread (TB, MAC, aspiration)
claims.quote: Tree-in-bud Chest CT Endobronchial spread (TB, MAC, aspiration)

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) MAC: so-called tree-and-bud infiltrates on chest CT are characteristic; on CXR, fibronodular infiltrates resemble TB, but cavitation is typically thin-walled and pleural effusion is rare
claims.quote: Fibronodular infiltrates on chest radiographs resemble those of pulmonary TB, but cavitation is typically thin-walled, and pleural effusion is rare. So-called tree-and-bud infiltrates, seen on chest CT, are also characteristic of MAC disease.

claims.text: Aspiration: infiltrate frequently (not exclusively) in dependent segments: superior or posterior basal segments of a lower lobe, or posterior segment of an upper lobe; aspiration-related abscess may show a cavity
claims.quote: For both chemical pneumonitis and aspiration pneumonia, chest radiographs show an infiltrate, frequently but not exclusively, in the dependent lung segments, ie, the superior or posterior basal segments of a lower lobe or the posterior segment of an upper lobe. For aspiration-related lung abscesses, chest radiographs may show a cavitary lesion.

claims.text: TB: in adults, a multinodular infiltrate above or behind the clavicle is most characteristic of active TB and suggests reactivation; best seen on an apical-lordotic view or chest CT
claims.quote: In adults, a multinodular infiltrate above or behind the clavicle is most characteristic of active TB; it suggests reactivation of disease. It is best visualized in an apical-lordotic view (a view designed to improve the visualization of the lung apices by elevating the clavicles) or on a chest CT scan.

claims.text: Causes NTM: disease usually requires a defect in local or systemic host defenses; highest risk with chronic lung disease (CF, bronchiectasis, COPD), HIV, frail older adults and immunocompromise
claims.quote: The occurrence of disease caused by NTM infections usually requires a defect in local or systemic host immune defenses. People at highest risk are those with chronic lung disease (including cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis due to causes other than cystic fibrosis, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), people with HIV infection, frail older adults, and immunocompromised patients, but others with less obvious immunocompromise can develop progressive disease (2).

claims.text: Mycobacterium avium complex (M. avium and M. intracellulare) accounts for most NTM disease
claims.quote: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) includes two closely related species, M. avium and M. intracellulare, and accounts for most NTM disease, but M. abscessus is increasingly becoming common globally (5).

claims.text: Aspiration risk factors: impaired consciousness (drug overdose, alcohol intoxication, seizures); dysphagia (esophageal/laryngeal or neurologic disease)
claims.quote: Risk factors for aspiration include: Impaired level of consciousness (eg, due to medication or illicit drug overdose, alcohol intoxication, seizures) Dysphagia (due to esophageal and/or laryngeal disorders, neurologic diseases)

claims.text: Symptoms MAC, one common scenario (Lady Windermere syndrome): immunocompetent, middle-aged or older White women with low BMI who have middle lobe bronchiectasis, scoliosis, pectus excavatum or MVP, typically presenting with a chronic nonproductive cough and no other lung abnormalities
claims.quote: One common clinical scenario of Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection is in immunocompetent, middle-aged or older, White women with a low BMI who have middle lobe bronchiectasis, scoliosis, pectus excavatum, or mitral valve prolapse. This patient population typically presents with a chronic nonproductive cough and no other lung abnormalities. This pattern is often called Lady Windermere syndrome

claims.text: Aspiration pneumonia: typically develops over hours to a few days (subacute with anaerobes); high-grade fever favors pneumonia over chemical pneumonitis
claims.quote: Aspiration pneumonia can have a variable onset depending on the underlying etiology. It typically develops over hours to a few days, and in cases caused by anaerobes, the evolution can be subacute. A high-grade fever is more suggestive of aspiration pneumonia rather than chemical pneumonitis.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: cultures; targeted therapy
MAC: sputum examination and culture diagnose it and distinguish it from TB
claims.quote: Sputum examination and culture are performed to diagnose MAC infection and to distinguish it from TB.

claims.text: NTM regimen (adults): usually azithromycin or clarithromycin + rifampin or rifabutin + ethambutol, continued for at least 12 months after culture conversion
claims.quote: Treatment of pulmonary disease in adults is tailored to the specific NTM species, disease severity, and drug susceptibility results (2). A 3-drug regimen, typically azithromycin or clarithromycin, rifampin (rifampicin) or rifabutin, and ethambutol, is recommended, sometimes with the addition of parenteral amikacin or streptomycin. Treatment should continue for at least 12 months after culture conversion.

claims.text: TB testing on sputum: acid-fast bacillus smear, NAATs and mycobacterial culture
claims.quote: Tests on sputum and other specimens: Microscopic examination of acid-fast bacillus stain smear; molecular tests (ie, nucleic acid amplification tests [NAATs]); and mycobacterial culture

claims.text: Community-acquired aspiration pneumonia: a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor (eg, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, ampicillin/sulbactam); moxifloxacin or clindamycin if penicillin-allergic
claims.quote: For community-acquired aspiration pneumonia, a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor (eg, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, ampicillin/sulbactam) is recommended; moxifloxacin or clindamycin is reserved for use in patients who are allergic to penicillin (6).
